words.def: To remove a need or difficulty, or to prevent a problem before it arises.
words.easy: Online check-in [obviates] the need to wait in line.
ex: Online check-in [obviates] the need to queue at the airport.
A clear contract would have [obviated] most of these disputes.
The new bridge [obviates] a two-hour detour.
words.nuance: Obviate almost always takes 'the need (for)': it makes something unnecessary. Preclude makes something impossible; avert turns away a danger that is coming.
words.ety: Late Latin obviare 'to meet in the way, prevent', from ob viam 'in the way'.

prec.s: Automatic backups ___ the need to save your work every five minutes.
prec.why: 'Obviate the need for' is the classic collocation: make something unnecessary. Preclude means make impossible; avert means turn away a danger; alleviate means ease suffering.

words.def: To prevent something from happening or make it impossible.
ex: His injury [precludes] him from playing in the final.
Lack of funding [precluded] any further research.
Being busy doesn't [preclude] being kind.
words.nuance: Preclude means circumstances make something impossible. Prohibit is an explicit ban by authority; rule out is deciding something is not an option.
words.ety: Latin praecludere 'to shut off', from claudere 'to close'.

prec.s: A full-time job doesn't ___ studying for a degree in the evenings.
prec.why: Preclude: make impossible by circumstances — and 'doesn't preclude' is very common. Prohibit and forbid are bans by authority; obviate means make unnecessary.

words.def: To find out something for certain, usually by investigating.
words.easy: Police are trying to [ascertain] what happened.
ex: Police are trying to [ascertain] the cause of the fire.
It's difficult to [ascertain] how many people were affected.
We need to [ascertain] whether the data are accurate.
words.nuance: Ascertain is formal 'find out for sure', common in official reports. Verify checks something already claimed; determine can also mean decide or cause.
words.ety: Old French acertener 'make certain', from certain.

prec.s: Investigators have not yet been able to ___ the cause of the crash.
prec.why: Ascertain means find out for certain. Assert means state firmly; assure means promise someone; assume means suppose without proof.

words.def: Having knowledge or awareness of something.
ex: We are [cognizant] of the risks involved.
Managers must be [cognizant] of their legal obligations.
She was fully [cognizant] that the decision would be unpopular.
words.nuance: Cognizant is a formal 'aware', typical of official or legal language. Mindful adds care and attention; conscious is everyday.
words.ety: Old French conoisance 'knowledge', from Latin cognoscere 'to get to know'.

prec.s: The board is fully ___ of its legal obligations to shareholders.
prec.why: Cognizant of = aware of. Cognitive relates to thinking processes; conscientious means diligent; conversant with means familiar with a subject through study.

words.def: Making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible.
ex: A noisy office is not [conducive] to concentration.
The warm climate is [conducive] to growing grapes.
We want an atmosphere [conducive] to open discussion.
words.nuance: Conducive always takes 'to' and describes conditions that help something happen. It's often negative: 'not conducive to sleep'.
words.ety: Latin conducere 'to bring together', from ducere 'to lead'.

prec.s: Loud music and bright screens are not ___ to a good night's sleep.
prec.why: Conducive to = helping something happen. Conductive describes metals conducting electricity; contingent on means depending on; consistent with means in agreement with.

words.def: Tending to cause harm.
ex: Lack of sleep is [detrimental] to your health.
The new rules could have a [detrimental] effect on small businesses.
He worked long hours to the [detriment] of his family life.
words.nuance: Detrimental is a neutral formal word for harmful; 'to the detriment of' means at the cost of. Pernicious is stronger and more moral.
words.ety: Latin detrimentum 'wearing away', from deterere 'to wear away'.

prec.s: Excessive screen time can be ___ to children's sleep and concentration.
prec.why: Detrimental to = harmful to. A deterrent discourages; a determinant decides an outcome; detached means separate or emotionally distant.

words.def: To make an action or process happen faster.
ex: Paying extra will [expedite] your passport application.
The new software has [expedited] the approval process.
We'll do what we can to [expedite] delivery.
words.nuance: Expedite is bureaucratic and business language for speeding up a process or order. Hasten is literary; accelerate is general.
words.ety: Latin expedire 'to free the feet', from pes, pedis 'foot'.

prec.s: For an extra fee, the embassy can ___ your visa application.
prec.why: Expedite means speed up a process. Expend means spend; expound means explain in detail; expunge means erase.

words.def: To delay or prevent progress by obstructing.
ex: Fallen trees [impeded] the rescue teams.
High taxes may [impede] economic growth.
His stammer was never an [impediment] to his career.
words.nuance: Impede means slow down or block movement or progress. Hamper suggests getting in the way; obstruct is more physical or deliberate (obstruct justice).
words.ety: Latin impedire 'to shackle the feet', from pes, pedis 'foot'.

prec.s: Heavy snow ___ the rescue teams as they climbed towards the stranded hikers.
prec.why: Impede means slow down by obstruction. Impel means drive someone to act; impose means force on someone; imply means suggest.

words.def: (adj., incumbent on) Necessary as a duty; (n.) the current holder of an office.
words.simple: The person who has an official job now.
ex: It is [incumbent] on parents to keep their children safe.
The [incumbent] lost the election by just 300 votes.
She is the [incumbent] mayor and is running again.
words.nuance: 'It is incumbent on someone to…' is a formal way to say they have a duty. As a noun, the incumbent is whoever currently holds the job, especially in elections.
words.ety: Latin incumbere 'to lie upon'.

prec.s: In local elections, the ___ usually has an advantage because voters already know her.
prec.why: The incumbent is the person currently in office. A candidate or nominee is anyone running; a predecessor held the office before.

words.def: A particular point in events or time, especially an important one.
words.simple: A point in time, often an important one.
ex: At this [juncture], it would be unwise to sell.
The talks have reached a critical [juncture].
At that [juncture], nobody knew the war would last five years.
words.nuance: Juncture is a formal word for a point in time, often a critical one. 'At this juncture' can sound pompous in casual speech.
words.ety: Latin iunctura 'joint', from iungere 'to join'.

prec.s: Negotiations have reached a critical ___; one wrong move could end them.
prec.why: A critical juncture is an important moment. A junction is where roads meet; a conjecture is a guess; a conjunction is a joining word or co-occurrence.

words.def: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; (of a person) able to think clearly.
ex: She gave a [lucid] explanation of a very complex topic.
The patient was weak but [lucid].
His writing is [lucid] and elegant.
words.nuance: Lucid praises clarity of thought or expression; for a person, it means mentally clear (often after confusion). Coherent means logically connected.
words.ety: Latin lucidus 'bright', from lux 'light'.

prec.s: Despite his high fever, he remained ___ and answered the doctor's questions clearly.
prec.why: Lucid means mentally clear. Lurid means shockingly vivid; lucrative means profitable; ludicrous means absurd.

words.def: Vague, unclear or ill-defined.
ex: The plan is still rather [nebulous].
'Synergy' is a [nebulous] concept that means different things to different people.
He had only a [nebulous] idea of what the job involved.
words.nuance: Nebulous criticises ideas or plans that lack a clear shape. Ambiguous means having two possible meanings; vague is the everyday word.
words.ety: Latin nebulosus 'cloudy', from nebula 'mist'.

prec.s: The CEO's ___ promise of 'transformation' left employees unsure what would actually change.
prec.why: Nebulous means vague and shapeless. Ambiguous means it could mean two specific things; ambivalent describes mixed feelings; obscure means little known or hard to understand.

words.def: A natural tendency to behave in a particular way.
words.simple: A natural habit of doing something.
words.easy: He has a [propensity] to talk too much.
ex: He has a [propensity] to exaggerate.
Teenagers have a higher [propensity] for risk-taking.
The [propensity] to save falls when interest rates are low.
words.nuance: Propensity is a formal, often negative or neutral tendency. A penchant is a liking (often charming); a proclivity is usually a tendency towards something bad.
words.ety: Latin propendere 'to hang forward, incline', from pendere 'to hang'.

prec.s: Economists study households' ___ to save rather than spend extra income.
prec.why: 'Propensity to save/consume' is a standard term in economics. A penchant is a fondness (a penchant for jazz); a predicament is a difficult situation; a prospect is a possibility.

words.def: A right or privilege that belongs to a particular person or group.
words.simple: A right that belongs to someone.
ex: It's your [prerogative] to change your mind.
Granting pardons is the president's [prerogative].
Choosing the team is the coach's [prerogative].
words.nuance: A prerogative is a right that comes with a role or position — or, informally, a personal choice nobody can dispute.
words.ety: Latin praerogativa 'the tribe voting first', from praerogare 'to ask first'.

prec.s: 'You don't have to come to the party — it's your ___,' she said.
prec.why: 'It's your prerogative' = it's your right to choose. A prerequisite is a requirement; a precedent is an earlier example; a pretext is a false reason.

words.def: A person who argues in favour of an idea or plan.
words.simple: A person who supports an idea.
words.easy: She's a [proponent] of working from home.
ex: She is a leading [proponent] of renewable energy.
[Proponents] of the plan say it will create jobs.
He was an early [proponent] of remote work.
words.nuance: A proponent argues for an idea in public debate. An advocate can also act for a person; an exponent is someone who promotes or skilfully performs something.
words.ety: Latin proponere 'to put forward', from ponere 'to place'.

prec.s: ___ of the four-day week argue that it boosts productivity.
prec.why: Proponents argue for an idea. Opponents argue against it; components are parts; exponents are mathematical powers or skilled performers of a style.

words.def: A state of uncertainty about what to do in a difficult situation.
words.easy: I'm in a [quandary] about the job offer.
ex: I'm in a [quandary] about whether to accept the job.
The judge faced a moral [quandary].
The new rules have left many parents in a [quandary].
words.nuance: A quandary is uncertainty about what to do. A dilemma involves a choice between two (often bad) options; a predicament is a difficult situation, not necessarily a choice.
words.ety: Uncertain; perhaps from Latin quando 'when'.

prec.s: Offered two jobs on the same day, she found herself in a happy ___.
prec.why: In a quandary = unsure what to do. A plight is a bad situation (no 'happy plight'); a quarrel is an argument; a quarry is a place for digging stone or a hunted animal.

words.def: Stubbornly uncooperative towards authority or discipline.
words.easy: The teacher had a few [recalcitrant] students.
ex: The teacher struggled with a few [recalcitrant] pupils.
[Recalcitrant] member states refused to sign the treaty.
Even the most [recalcitrant] stains came out.
words.nuance: Recalcitrant specifically resists authority or control. Obstinate is general stubbornness; intransigent refuses compromise in negotiations.
words.ety: Latin recalcitrare 'to kick back', from calx 'heel' — like a mule.

prec.s: The new head teacher was determined to deal firmly with ___ pupils who ignored every rule.
prec.why: Recalcitrant means defying authority — fitting pupils who ignore rules. Intransigent refuses compromise in negotiations; tenacious and resolute are positive.

words.def: A cancellation or postponement of a punishment; a temporary relief from something bad.
words.easy: The rain gave us a [reprieve] from the heat.
ex: The factory won a [reprieve] when a buyer was found.
The rain gave us a brief [reprieve] from the heat.
The prisoner was [reprieved] hours before the execution.
words.nuance: A reprieve is relief from something bad that was going to happen (closure, punishment). A respite is a short rest from something ongoing.
words.ety: Anglo-French repris 'taken back'.

prec.s: The library, due to close next month, won a last-minute ___ when a local firm offered funding.
prec.why: A reprieve cancels or postpones a threatened bad outcome. A respite is a short rest from something unpleasant that continues; remission is a period when a disease improves; a refund returns money.

words.def: Happening occasionally and irregularly, not continuously.
words.simple: Happening now and then, not regularly.
ex: There has been [sporadic] fighting in the north.
Her attendance was [sporadic] at best.
We heard [sporadic] gunfire during the night.
words.nuance: Sporadic stresses unpredictable, scattered occurrences. Intermittent means stopping and starting, often more regularly (intermittent rain).
words.ety: Greek sporadikos 'scattered', from speirein 'to sow'.

prec.s: Despite the ceasefire, there were ___ reports of shooting in remote villages.
prec.why: Sporadic means scattered and occasional. Chronic means long-lasting; incessant means non-stop; perennial means recurring year after year.

words.def: (Of rules or conditions) strict, precise and demanding.
ex: Food producers must meet [stringent] safety standards.
The loan comes with [stringent] conditions.
Security checks have become more [stringent].
words.nuance: Stringent is neutral or approving: demanding rules that are rigorously applied. Draconian criticises rules as excessively harsh.
words.ety: Latin stringere 'to draw tight'.

prec.s: Baby food must meet ___ safety standards, with tests on every batch.
prec.why: Stringent standards are strict and demanding — appropriately so here. Draconian criticises rules as cruel; austere means plain and severe; strident means harsh and loud.

words.def: (tantamount to) Equivalent in seriousness or effect to.
words.simple: Almost the same as something bad.
ex: Refusing to answer is [tantamount] to admitting guilt.
The new tax is [tantamount] to theft, critics say.
His silence was [tantamount] to approval.
words.nuance: Tantamount to is used to say something is as bad as something else, usually a strong accusation. Don't confuse with paramount (most important).
words.ety: Anglo-French tant amunter 'amount to as much'.

prec.s: Refusing to release the documents is ___ to admitting there is something to hide.
prec.why: Tantamount to = as good as, equivalent to. Paramount means most important; commensurate with means proportionate to; conducive to means helping something happen.

words.def: Capable of working successfully; feasible.
ex: Solar power is now a [viable] alternative to coal.
The business is no longer financially [viable].
Is there a [viable] way to cut costs without layoffs?
words.nuance: Viable means able to survive or work in practice, often economically. Feasible means possible to do; plausible means seeming true.
words.ety: French viable, from vie 'life' — capable of living.

prec.s: Without government subsidies, the small airline is no longer financially ___.
prec.why: 'Financially viable' = able to survive economically. Plausible means believable; valid means legally or logically acceptable; vital means essential.

words.def: To reach a climax or final point after a gradual development.
words.simple: To end in a big final moment.
ex: Years of protest [culminated] in a change of government.
The festival [culminates] with fireworks on Saturday night.
The award was the [culmination] of a long career.
words.nuance: Culminate in/with is about a build-up reaching its high point. Result in is neutral cause and effect; come to a head is informal, for a crisis.
words.ety: Late Latin culminare, from culmen 'summit'.

prec.s: Months of rising tension ___ in a general strike that shut down the country.
prec.why: Culminate in = reach a climax in. Accumulate means build up gradually (and doesn't take 'in'); calculate means work out; cultivate means grow or develop.

words.def: Polite submission and respect towards someone's opinion, age or authority.
words.simple: Respect shown by doing what someone wants.
words.easy: In [deference] to her wishes, we stayed quiet.
ex: In [deference] to his wishes, the funeral was private.
The young doctors treated the professor with great [deference].
Out of [deference] to her grandmother, she wore a skirt.
words.nuance: Deference is respect that makes you yield to someone else's wishes or authority. Reverence is deep admiration, often religious.
words.ety: French déférence, from déférer 'to refer, yield'.

prec.s: In ___ to the family's wishes, the funeral was kept private.
prec.why: 'In deference to' someone's wishes = out of respect for them. Difference is dissimilarity; defiance is open resistance; 'in reference to' means regarding.

words.def: A lack of agreement or harmony; an unpleasant clash of sounds or ideas.
words.simple: A feeling that two things don't fit together.
words.easy: There's a [dissonance] between what he says and does.
ex: Smokers who know the risks experience cognitive [dissonance].
There's a [dissonance] between the company's values and its behaviour.
The composer uses [dissonance] to create tension.
words.nuance: Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort of holding contradictory beliefs or acting against them. Discord is disagreement between people.
words.ety: Latin dissonare 'to disagree in sound', from sonare 'to sound'.

prec.s: Eating meat while loving animals creates what psychologists call cognitive ___.
prec.why: 'Cognitive dissonance' is the fixed term. Discord is conflict between people; dissent is disagreement with authority; distortion is a twisting of facts.

words.def: A perfect example of a quality or type.
ex: She is the [epitome] of elegance.
The hotel is the [epitome] of luxury.
His behaviour [epitomized] everything that was wrong with the company.
words.nuance: Epitome is used in 'the epitome of + quality'. Note the pronunciation: four syllables, ih-PIT-uh-mee.
words.ety: Greek epitomē 'abridgement', from epitemnein 'to cut short'.

prec.s: With its marble halls and gold taps, the hotel is the ___ of luxury.
prec.why: The epitome of = the perfect example of. An epitaph is a gravestone inscription; an epicentre is the centre of an earthquake or crisis; an episode is one part of a series.

words.def: Something that makes a process happen or happen more quickly; driving force.
words.simple: Something that makes things start or move faster.
words.easy: The crisis gave new [impetus] to the plan.
ex: The scandal gave new [impetus] to the reform movement.
The [impetus] for change came from employees.
The talks have lost their [impetus].
words.nuance: Impetus is the push that starts or speeds something. Momentum is the force something has once moving; an incentive is a reward that motivates.
words.ety: Latin impetus 'assault, force', from impetere 'to attack'.

prec.s: The disaster provided the ___ for long-overdue safety reforms.
prec.why: The impetus for = the driving force behind. Impetuous is an adjective meaning rash; an imprint is a mark; an impasse is a deadlock.

words.def: Not resulting from or achieved through deliberate planning; unintentional.
ex: I [inadvertently] deleted the whole file.
The leak was [inadvertent], the company insists.
She made an [inadvertent] error in the calculations.
words.nuance: Inadvertent stresses lack of intention, often from not paying attention. Unwitting means not knowing what you were doing or part of.
words.ety: in- 'not' + Latin advertere 'to turn towards', from vertere 'to turn'.

prec.s: I ___ replied to everyone in the company instead of just my manager.
prec.why: Inadvertently = by accident. Inadequately means not well enough; indefinitely means with no fixed end; invariably means always.

words.def: Present from birth; natural rather than learned.
words.easy: She has an [innate] sense of rhythm.
ex: Children have an [innate] ability to learn languages.
She has an [innate] sense of rhythm.
Is aggression [innate] or learned?
words.nuance: Innate is for qualities of people and animals present from birth. Inherent is for qualities of things and systems (inherent risk).
words.ety: Latin innatus 'inborn', from nasci 'to be born'.

prec.s: Some researchers believe humans have an ___ capacity for language that needs no teaching.
prec.why: Innate describes abilities present from birth in living beings. Inherent and intrinsic are mostly about the nature of things or ideas; endemic means regularly found in a place.

words.def: Lacking interest or excitement; ordinary and everyday.
ex: She was tired of [mundane] tasks like filing and photocopying.
Even the most [mundane] objects can be beautiful in a photograph.
The conversation drifted to [mundane] matters like parking.
words.nuance: Mundane means everyday and unexciting — not necessarily bad. Banal suggests something unoriginal and boring; humdrum is informal and monotonous.
words.ety: Latin mundanus 'worldly', from mundus 'world'.

prec.s: Astronauts say that even in space, much of their time is spent on ___ chores like cleaning.
prec.why: Mundane means ordinary and everyday. Profane means irreverent; 'mundial' isn't an English word (Spanish for 'world'); lucid means clear.

words.def: Involving a great deal of effort, trouble or difficulty; burdensome.
ex: Small firms complain about [onerous] paperwork.
The loan came with [onerous] conditions.
Caring for him alone was an [onerous] task.
words.nuance: Onerous is about burdens and obligations that weigh on you, often legal or administrative. Arduous is about physically or mentally exhausting effort.
words.ety: Latin onerosus, from onus 'burden'.

prec.s: Small businesses say the new reporting rules are ___, requiring hours of paperwork every week.
prec.why: Onerous fits obligations and rules that are a burden. Arduous suits hard physical or mental effort (an arduous climb); ominous means threatening; odious means hateful.

words.def: Designed to impress or attract attention, especially by showing wealth.
ex: They live in an [ostentatious] mansion with gold taps.
He wore an [ostentatious] watch to the meeting.
Despite her wealth, she avoided [ostentatious] displays.
words.nuance: Ostentatious criticises showing off wealth or importance. Flamboyant is about a bold, colourful style or personality, often admired.
words.ety: Latin ostentare 'to display', from ostendere 'to show'.

prec.s: The billionaire's ___ yacht, with its own helicopter pad, drew criticism during the recession.
prec.why: Ostentatious = showy, flaunting wealth. Ostensible means apparent; obsequious means servile; ominous means threatening.

words.def: So intense or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt.
words.simple: So strong you can almost touch it.
words.easy: The fear in the room was [palpable].
ex: The tension in the room was [palpable].
There was a [palpable] sense of relief when the results came in.
His fear was [palpable].
words.nuance: Palpable is used for atmospheres and feelings so strong you can almost touch them. Tangible is for real, concrete benefits or evidence.
words.ety: Late Latin palpabilis, from palpare 'to touch gently'.

prec.s: As the jury returned, the tension in the courtroom was ___.
prec.why: 'The tension was palpable' is the classic collocation. Tangible suits concrete benefits or evidence; palatable means tasty or acceptable; pliable means easily bent.

words.def: Optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation.
ex: The minister was [sanguine] about the economy's prospects.
I'm not as [sanguine] as you are about our chances.
Investors remain surprisingly [sanguine] despite the warnings.
words.nuance: Sanguine often implies optimism others may think unjustified; it's common in the negative ('less sanguine'). Upbeat is informal.
words.ety: Latin sanguineus 'of blood' — a blood-dominated temperament was thought cheerful.

prec.s: Analysts are less ___ than the government about the chances of avoiding a recession.
prec.why: Sanguine = optimistic. Sanguinary means bloody (a sanguinary battle); sanctimonious means self-righteous; sardonic means mocking.

words.def: To examine or inspect closely and thoroughly.
words.simple: To look at something very carefully.
ex: Auditors will [scrutinize] every expense claim.
She [scrutinized] his face for any sign of lying.
The deal is now under close [scrutiny].
words.nuance: Scrutinize means examine critically, looking for faults. Peruse traditionally means read carefully, but is often used to mean skim.
words.ety: Late Latin scrutinium 'search', from scrutari 'to search through rubbish'.

prec.s: Before signing, the lawyer ___ every clause of the contract.
prec.why: Scrutinize means examine closely and critically. Skim, glance at and browse are all quick and superficial.

words.def: To demand or specify something as part of an agreement or rule.
words.simple: To say clearly what must be done in a deal.
ex: The contract [stipulates] that payment must be made within 30 days.
Her will [stipulated] that the house could not be sold.
One [stipulation] of the loan is that you keep the property insured.
words.nuance: Stipulate is used for conditions in contracts, laws and wills. Specify is more general (specify the size).
words.ety: Latin stipulari 'to demand as a formal promise'.

prec.s: The lease ___ that tenants may not keep pets.
prec.why: Stipulate = set as a condition in an agreement. Stimulate means encourage; speculate means guess; simulate means imitate.

words.def: In exactly the same words as were used originally.
ex: He repeated her instructions [verbatim].
The newspaper printed the letter [verbatim].
We need a [verbatim] record of the meeting.
words.nuance: Verbatim is about copying exact words. Literally means in the literal sense — often misused as an intensifier.
words.ety: Medieval Latin, from verbum 'word'.

prec.s: The student was caught copying whole paragraphs ___ from Wikipedia.
prec.why: Verbatim = word for word. Verbosely means using too many words; vicariously means through someone else's experience; virtually means almost.

words.def: Having or showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or objective, sometimes excessively.
words.simple: Very eager and full of energy for something.
ex: The [zealous] new manager rewrote every procedure.
Police were accused of being over-[zealous] in enforcing the curfew.
She is a [zealous] defender of free speech.
words.nuance: Zealous can be admiring or warn of excess; 'over-zealous' is clearly critical. A zealot is a fanatic.
words.ety: Greek zēlos 'eagerness, jealousy' (the same source as 'jealous').

prec.s: An over-___ security guard refused to let the CEO into her own building without ID.
prec.why: Over-zealous means too enthusiastic in applying rules. Jealous shares the origin but means envious; pious means religious; candid means honest.

words.def: Having or showing a strong wish for revenge.
ex: Her ex-husband was [vindictive] and tried to ruin her business.
The sacking looked like a [vindictive] act.
Don't be [vindictive] — let it go.
words.nuance: Vindictive is about wanting revenge. Spiteful is small-scale meanness; malicious is intent to harm, not necessarily revenge. Don't confuse with vindicated (proved right).
words.ety: Latin vindicta 'vengeance'.

prec.s: After she left the company, her ___ former boss tried to stop her getting any job in the industry.
prec.why: Vindictive = seeking revenge. Vindicated means proved right; vigilant means watchful; venerable means respected for age.

words.def: Feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems.
words.simple: Careful because something might be dangerous.
ex: Be [wary] of emails asking for your password.
Investors are [wary] of the new market.
The cat watched the dog [warily].
words.nuance: Wary adds a hint of suspicion to caution. Weary means tired — a frequent confusion.
words.ety: Old English wær 'aware, careful' (same root as 'beware').

prec.s: After being scammed once, she was ___ of any email that asked for her bank details.
prec.why: Wary of = cautious and suspicious about. Weary means tired; wry means drily amused; wan means pale.
